questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Linear Polynomials
questions.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ 4 & 1 & 3 \\  & ↓ & 4 \\  & 1 & 7\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{x+3}{x-4}=1+\frac{7}{x-4}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+3}{x-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{7}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+7\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+7\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
questions.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 3 & -4 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{9}{2} \\  & 3 & -\frac{17}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} & =3-\frac{(\frac{17}{2})}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{17}{2x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-17{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[3x-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3(2-0)-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(2)+3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(0)+3|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3})] \\  & =3-\frac{17}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x+3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x+3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\  & 1 & -4\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x+3)} & =1+\frac{(-4)}{(x+3)} \\  & =1-\frac{4}{(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & \frac{2}{3} \\  & 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3x-2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-\frac{1}{3x-2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C.\end{aligned}
